items.title: Q1 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden
items.stem:
"When nature prompted and no law denied
Promiscuous use of concubine and bride;
Then Israel's monarch after Heaven's own heart,
His vigorous warmth did variously impart
To wives and slaves."
From which poem are these lines taken?
options: A Song for St. Cecilia's Day
items.explanation: These lines are the famous opening verses (lines 5–9) of John Dryden's Biblical-political satire Absalom and Achitophel: A Poem (1681), which allegorizes King Charles II as King David ('Israel's monarch') and the Earl of Shaftesbury as Achitophel during the Exclusion Crisis.

items.title: Q2 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which of the following poems is written by Oliver Goldsmith?
items.explanation: The Deserted Village (1770) is a famous pastoral elegiac poem in heroic couplets by Oliver Goldsmith, lamenting rural depopulation and the enclosure of the idyllic village of Auburn.

items.title: Q3 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Mamta Kalia
items.stem: Tribute to Papa is a book of poems written by
items.explanation: Tribute to Papa and Other Poems (1970), published by P. Lal's Writers Workshop in Calcutta, is the acclaimed debut English poetry collection of Indian writer Mamta Kalia.

items.title: Q4 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Sylvia Plath
items.stem: Which of the following poems is not written by Sylvia Plath?
items.explanation: 'Lady Lazarus', 'Ariel', and 'Daddy' are iconic confessional poems by Sylvia Plath collected in her posthumous volume Ariel (1965), whereas 'To Ariel' is not written by Sylvia Plath.

items.title: Q5 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Burns
items.stem: Robert Burns was born in
items.explanation: Robert Burns (1759–1796), celebrated as the national poet of Scotland and a key figure of the Pre-Romantic movement, was born in Alloway, Ayrshire, Scotland.

items.title: Q6 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit I: Drama · Percy Bysshe Shelley
items.stem: Who among the following characters personifies necessity in P. B. Shelley's Prometheus Unbound?
items.explanation: In Percy Bysshe Shelley's four-act lyrical drama Prometheus Unbound (1820), the mysterious primal spirit Demogorgon personifies historical and cosmic Necessity, rising from the abyss in Act III to overthrow the tyrannical Jupiter (Jove).

items.title: Q7 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare, Samuel Pepys
items.stem: Who among the following, after watching the performance of William Shakespeare's play, A Midsummer Night's Dream, observed that "it is the most insipid, ridiculous play that I ever saw in my life."
items.explanation: In his diary entry for 29 September 1662, Restoration diarist Samuel Pepys recorded watching a performance of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream at the King's Theatre and dismissed it as 'the most insipid ridiculous play that ever I saw in my life.'

items.title: Q8 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Name the playwright who wrote the play Epicene, or the Silent Woman?
items.explanation: Epicoene, or The Silent Woman (1609) is a Renaissance city comedy written by Ben Jonson, centering on the noise-hating miser Morose and his nephew Sir Dauphine Eugenie.

items.title: Q9 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Kalidasa
items.stem: Abhijnanasakuntalam makes use of the following four languages
items.explanation: Kalidasa's classical drama Abhijnanasakuntalam follows Natyashastra linguistic conventions by employing Sanskrit for the king and courtiers alongside three dramatic Prakrits: Shauraseni (for women and the vidushaka), Maharashtri (for lyric verses), and Magadhi (for guards and the fisherman).

items.title: Q10 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · John Osborne, Arnold Wesker, Shelagh Delaney, John Arden
items.stem: Choose from the following options the correct combination of playwrights who contributed to the movement called "Kitchen Sink Drama".
options: John Osborne, Arnold Wesker, Shelagh Delaney and John Arden
John Osborne, Arnold Wesker, Harold Pinter and Shelagh Delaney
John Osborne, Arnold Wesker, Antonin Artaud and John Arden
John Osborne, Harold Pinter, Shelagh Delaney and John Arden
items.explanation: John Osborne (Look Back in Anger), Arnold Wesker (The Wesker Trilogy), Shelagh Delaney (A Taste of Honey), and John Arden (Live Like Pigs) were key British 'Kitchen Sink' social-realist playwrights of the late 1950s, whereas Harold Pinter is associated with the Comedy of Menace and Antonin Artaud with the Theatre of Cruelty.

items.title: Q11 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit I: Drama · Eugene O'Neill, Elmer Rice
items.stem: Choose from the following options the correct combination of the plays which made significant use of expressionistic techniques:
options: The Hairy Ape, Machinal, All My Sons, Waiting for Lefty
The Hairy Ape, The Crucible, Rapid Transit, The Adding Machine
The Hairy Ape, Rapid Transit, All My Sons, The Adding Machine
The Hairy Ape, The Emperor Jones, Rapid Transit, The Adding Machine
items.explanation: Eugene O'Neill's The Hairy Ape (1922) and The Emperor Jones (1920), Lajos Egri's Rapid Transit (1927), and Elmer Rice's The Adding Machine (1923) all made pioneering use of Expressionist theatrical techniques, whereas Arthur Miller's All My Sons and The Crucible are realist plays.

items.title: Q12 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · Bertolt Brecht
items.stem: Apart from Bertolt Brecht others who have influenced Epic theatre are:
items.explanation: Alongside Bertolt Brecht, German theatre directors Erwin Piscator (who pioneered political documentary and Epic staging techniques in the 1920s) and Max Reinhardt (for his large-scale theatrical innovations) significantly influenced the development of Epic theatre.

items.title: Q13 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Richard Hooker
items.stem: The theological treatise Ecclesiastical Polity was written by
items.explanation: Of the Lawes of Ecclesiasticall Politie (first four books published in 1594) was written by the Elizabethan Anglican theologian Richard Hooker, defending the theology and governance of the Church of England against Puritan critiques.

items.title: Q14 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Izaak Walton
items.stem: Who wrote the popular instruction manual for fishermen titled The Compleat Angler, or The Contemplative Man's Recreation?
items.explanation: First published in 1653, The Compleat Angler, or the Contemplative Man's Recreation was written by Izaak (Isaac) Walton as a pastoral dialogue celebrating the art and philosophy of fishing.

items.title: Q15 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: What did Matthew Arnold imply by the term "Hebraism" in his Culture and Anarchy?
items.explanation: In Chapter IV ('Hebraism and Hellenism') of Culture and Anarchy (1869), Matthew Arnold defines Hebraism as the spirit of strictness of conscience, duty, obedience, and moral conduct or moral education, in contrast to Hellenism's intellectual spontaneity ('seeing things as they really are').

items.title: Q16 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · F. R. Leavis
items.stem: The journal Scrutiny was founded in 1932 by
items.explanation: The influential quarterly critical journal Scrutiny (1932–1953) was founded at Cambridge in 1932 by L.C. Knights and F.R. Leavis, with F.R. Leavis serving as its chief editor and intellectual driving force.

items.title: Q17 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Pepys
items.stem: Samuel Pepys' claim to fame rests on his
items.explanation: Samuel Pepys (1633–1703) is famous for his private Diary, kept in shorthand from 1660 to 1669, which provides a vivid eyewitness account of Restoration London, the Great Plague of 1665, the Great Fire of 1666, and the Restoration stage.

items.title: Q18 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Dr Primrose is a character in
items.explanation: Dr. Charles Primrose is the kind-hearted, unworldly country clergyman who serves as the narrator and protagonist of Oliver Goldsmith's sentimental novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766).

items.title: Q19 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem:
"So the baby was carried in a small deal box, under an ancient woman's shawl, to the churchyard that night, and buried by lantern-light, at the cost of a shilling, and a pint of beer to the sexton, in that shabby corner of God's allotment where He lets the nettles grow, and where all unbaptized infants, notorious drunkards, suicides and others of the conjecturally damned are laid."
From which novel is this excerpt taken?
options: Mill on the Floss by George Eliot
items.explanation: This passage occurs at the end of Phase the Second (Chapter XIV) of Thomas Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), describing the midnight burial of Tess's illegitimate infant son, Sorrow, after the local parson refuses him a Christian burial.

items.title: Q20 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Patrick White
items.stem: Which of the following novels is written by Patrick White?
items.explanation: The Vivisector (1970), charting the lifelong artistic obsession of the fictional Australian painter Hurtle Duffield, was written by Nobel Prize-winning Australian novelist Patrick White. Cry, the Beloved Country is by Alan Paton, The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood, and The Stone Angel by Margaret Laurence.

items.title: Q21 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Kamala Markandaya, Nayantara Sahgal
items.stem: Which among the following is NOT written by Kamala Markandaya?
items.explanation: A Time to Be Happy (1958) was written by Indian English novelist Nayantara Sahgal, not Kamala Markandaya. Some Inner Fury (1955), The Nowhere Man (1972), and The Golden Honeycomb (1977) are all novels by Kamala Markandaya.

items.title: Q22 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams
items.stem: Who among the following were revaluing 'the masses' as sources and subjects of literature?
items.explanation: In foundational British Cultural Studies works such as The Uses of Literacy (1957) and Culture and Society (1958), Richard Hoggart and Raymond Williams challenged elitist dismissals of 'the masses' and revalued working-class life and popular culture as vital subjects of study.

items.title: Q23 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Who among the following theorists has written on narrative empathy?
items.explanation: American literary theorist Suzanne Keen formulated the theory of narrative empathy in her influential article 'A Theory of Narrative Empathy' (2006) and her book Empathy and the Novel (2007), examining how fictional techniques evoke reader empathy.

items.title: Q24 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: The science that systematically studies the function of signs is known as
items.explanation: Coined by Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure in his Course in General Linguistics (1916), semiology (or semiotics) is the general science that systematically studies the life and function of signs within society.

items.title: Q25 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Who among the following first framed a theory of general hermeneutics?
items.explanation: German philosopher and theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768–1834) is regarded as the father of modern general hermeneutics, expanding interpretation beyond specialized biblical and legal exegesis into a universal theory of linguistic and psychological understanding.

items.title: Q26 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes
items.stem: Roland Barthes' Image, Music, Text was published in
items.explanation: Image-Music-Text, the influential English-language collection of Roland Barthes's structuralist and poststructuralist essays (including 'The Death of the Author' and 'From Work to Text') selected and translated by Stephen Heath, was published in 1977.

items.title: Q27 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Who among the following distinguished the 'constatives' from the 'performatives'?
items.explanation: British ordinary-language philosopher J.L. (John Langshaw) Austin introduced the distinction between 'constative' utterances (statements that describe facts and are true or false) and 'performative' utterances (speech acts that perform an action) in How to Do Things with Words (1962).

items.title: Q28 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Who among the following coined the phrase 'soft capitalism'?
items.explanation: British cultural geographer and social theorist Nigel Thrift coined and popularized the phrase 'soft capitalism' in his 1997 essay 'The Rise of Soft Capitalism' (and his 2005 book Knowing Capitalism) to describe modern management-driven, knowledge-based corporate capitalism.

items.title: Q29 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: To whom is the term 'thick description' attributed?
items.explanation: American cultural anthropologist Clifford Geertz adapted the term 'thick description' (originally coined by philosopher Gilbert Ryle) in his landmark work The Interpretation of Cultures (1973) to describe interpreting human behavior within its rich web of cultural context, a method later adopted by New Historicists.

items.title: Q30 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: The subject matter of Cultural Studies as it emerged as a 'proto-discipline' in the 1960s, was predominantly exploration of
items.explanation: When Cultural Studies emerged as a proto-discipline in the 1960s (particularly with the founding of the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies in 1964), its predominant subject matter was the serious critical exploration of popular and working-class culture.

items.title: Q31 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Richard Hoggart, Stuart Hall
items.stem: What does the abbreviated term CCCS stand for in the context of cultural studies?
options: Consortium of Cooperative Culture and Society
Conference on Contemporary Culture and Society
Conclave for Collective Consciousness and Socialisation
items.explanation: In Cultural Studies, CCCS stands for the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, a landmark research center founded by Richard Hoggart in 1964 at the University of Birmingham and later directed by Stuart Hall.

items.title: Q32 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stuart Hall
items.stem: According to Stuart Hall, the concept of ________ played a seminal role in Cultural Studies.
items.explanation: According to Stuart Hall, Antonio Gramsci's concept of cultural 'hegemony'—the process by which ruling groups win and negotiate consent across civil society and popular culture—played a seminal theoretical role in shaping Cultural Studies.

items.title: Q33 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · William Shakespeare
items.stem: The book Political Shakespeare: Essays in Cultural Materialism was jointly edited by
items.explanation: Political Shakespeare: New Essays in Cultural Materialism (1985), a foundational anthology of British Cultural Materialism, was jointly edited by Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield.

items.title: Q34 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: Identify the work which has NOT been authored by the famous cultural critic Raymond Williams:
options: The Making of the English Working Class
items.explanation: The Making of the English Working Class (1963) was written by British Marxist historian E.P. Thompson, not Raymond Williams. The Country and the City (1973), Culture and Society (1958), and Modern Tragedy (1966) were all authored by Raymond Williams.

items.title: Q35 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Second Language is
options: the language second in importance in terms of the use of languages by a learner.
the language used by a second generation learner.
any language other than the learner's native language or mother tongue.
the language which is the learner's native language but not the mother tongue.
items.explanation: In Second Language Acquisition (SLA) and applied linguistics, a 'second language' (L2) is defined broadly as any language learned after and in addition to the learner's native language or mother tongue (L1).

items.title: Q36 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: When a learner's second language learning system seems to freeze or get stuck at some more or less deviant stage, that phenomenon is known as
items.explanation: Introduced by Larry Selinker in his 1972 paper 'Interlanguage,' fossilization refers to the phenomenon in second-language acquisition where a learner's interlanguage system freezes or permanently stops progressing toward native-like target language norms.

items.title: Q37 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Integrative motivation refers to
options: language learning for personal growth and cultural enrichment.
items.explanation: In Robert Gardner and Wallace Lambert's (1972) socio-educational model of second-language acquisition, integrative motivation refers to learning a language for personal growth, cultural enrichment, and a desire to integrate with the target language community, as opposed to instrumental motivation.

items.title: Q38 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: In 1835, which of the following languages was replaced by English as the official language of the East India Company?
items.explanation: In 1835, under Governor-General Lord William Bentinck, English replaced Persian as the official administrative and diplomatic language of the British East India Company in India.

items.title: Q39 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Charles Wood
items.stem: Choose the correct option from the following options:
options: The "Magna Carta" of Indian Education in the colonial period refers to "The Missionary Clause 1698"
The "Magna Carta" of Indian Education in the colonial period refers to "Indian Education Commission in 1882".
The "Magna Carta" of Indian Education in the colonial period refers to "Macaulay's Minute 1835".
The "Magna Carta" of Indian Education in the colonial period refers to "Wood's Education Despatch of 1854".
items.explanation: Sir Charles Wood's Education Despatch of 1854 (sent to Governor-General Lord Dalhousie) is famously known as the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India' because it laid out the first comprehensive plan for mass primary, secondary, and university education across colonial India.

items.title: Q40 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare, Girish Chandra Ghosh
items.stem: Which of the following plays of William Shakespeare was translated into Bengali and directed by Girish Chandra Ghosh.
items.explanation: Pioneering Bengali playwright, actor, and director Girish Chandra Ghosh translated William Shakespeare's tragedy Macbeth into Bengali and staged it at the Minerva Theatre in Calcutta in January 1893.

items.title: Q41 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit I: Drama · Robert Browning
items.stem:
Which of the following works of Browning are pure dramas?
A. Strafford
B. The Last Ride Together
C. A Blot in the 'Scutcheon
D. Pippa Passes
E. Porphyria's Lover
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Strafford (1837, A) and A Blot in the 'Scutcheon (1843, C) are full-length stage tragedies ('pure dramas') written by Robert Browning, whereas 'The Last Ride Together' and 'Porphyria's Lover' are dramatic monologues and Pippa Passes is a verse closet drama of linked scenes.

items.title: Q42 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Judith Wright, Yusef Komunyakaa, Oodgeroo Noonuccal (Kath Walker)
items.stem:
Who among the following poets have lived in Australia?
A. Judith Wright
B. Yusef Komunyakaa
C. Kath Walker
D. Thomas Kinsella
E. T. S. Eliot
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Judith Wright (A) and Aboriginal poet Kath Walker / Oodgeroo Noonuccal (C) were native Australian poets, and African American Pulitzer Prize-winning poet Yusef Komunyakaa (B) lived in Australia for over a decade beginning in the mid-1980s.

items.title: Q43 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
In An Essay on Criticism, Pope
A. analyses the causes of faulty criticism and praises the great critics of the past.
B. analyses the causes of faulty criticism and characterises the good critic
C. analyses the structure of a good essay and praises the great critics of the past.
D. analyses the structure of a good essay and suggest how such an essay could be converted into good criticism.
E. analyses the merits of the poetry of Wordsworth and praises the great critics of the past.
Which of the above statements are correct?
items.explanation: In An Essay on Criticism (1711), Alexander Pope analyzes the causes of faulty criticism (such as pride, imperfect learning, and pedantry in Part II), characterizes the qualities of the ideal critic, and praises the great critics of antiquity and the Renaissance in Part III (A and B).

items.title: Q44 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter
items.stem:
Which of the following are plays written by Harold Pinter?
A. Family Voices
B. A Moon for the Misbegotten
C. The Room
D. No Man's Land
E. Krapp's Last Tape
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Family Voices (1981, A), The Room (1957, C), and No Man's Land (1975, D) are plays written by British dramatist Harold Pinter. A Moon for the Misbegotten (1947) is by Eugene O'Neill, and Krapp's Last Tape (1958) is by Samuel Beckett.

items.title: Q45 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Mahesh Dattani, Girish Karnad
items.stem:
Which of the following have NOT been written by Mahesh Dattani?
A. Dance Like a Man
B. Fire and the Rain
C. On A Muggy Night in Mumbai
D. A Touch of Brightness
E. Bravely Fought the Queen
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Fire and the Rain (1998, B) was written by Girish Karnad and A Touch of Brightness (1968, D) was written by Partap Sharma. Dance Like a Man (1989), On a Muggy Night in Mumbai (1998), and Bravely Fought the Queen (1991) are plays by Mahesh Dattani.

items.title: Q46 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Harold Pinter, Samuel Beckett, Eugene Ionesco
items.stem:
Name the dramas which fall within the category of the Theatre of the Absurd.
A. The Birthday Party
B. Endgame
C. Mrs. Warren's Profession
D. The Rhinoceros
E. Riders to the Sea
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Harold Pinter's The Birthday Party (1957, A), Samuel Beckett's Endgame (1957, B), and Eugène Ionesco's Rhinoceros (1959, D) are canonical plays of the Theatre of the Absurd. Mrs. Warren's Profession is a realist problem play by G.B. Shaw, and Riders to the Sea is an Irish folk tragedy by J.M. Synge.

items.title: Q47 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson, Aphra Behn, Richard Brinsley Sheridan
items.stem:
Which of the playwrights have been correctly matched with their works?
A. William Wycherly – The Rivals
B. Ben Jonson – Volpone, or the Fox
C. William Congreve – The Country Wife
D. Aphra Behn – The Dutch Lover
E. Richard Sheridan – A School for Scandal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Ben Jonson wrote Volpone, or The Fox (1606, B), Aphra Behn wrote The Dutch Lover (1673, D), and Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote The School for Scandal (1777, E). The Rivals (1775) was written by Sheridan (not Wycherley), and The Country Wife (1675) was written by William Wycherley (not Congreve).

items.title: Q48 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit I: Drama · Lord Byron
items.stem:
Choose the plays written by Lord Byron
A. Sardanapalus
B. Hellas
C. Cain
D. The Two Foscari: An Historical Tragedy
E. The Cenci
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Sardanapalus (A), Cain: A Mystery (C), and The Two Foscari: An Historical Tragedy (D) are closet dramas by Lord Byron published together in a single volume in December 1821. Hellas (1822) and The Cenci (1819) were written by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

items.title: Q49 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Bunyan
items.stem:
John Bunyan authored the following:
A. The Pilgrim's Progress
B. Grace Abounding
C. Short View
D. The Holy War
E. Thoughts on Education
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Puritan preacher and allegorist John Bunyan authored The Pilgrim's Progress (1678, A), the spiritual autobiography Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666, B), and The Holy War (1682, D). A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage is by Jeremy Collier, and Some Thoughts Concerning Education is by John Locke.

items.title: Q50 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas De Quincey
items.stem:
Which of the following works have been authored by Thomas De Quincey?
A. Confessions of An English Opium Eater
B. The French Revolution
C. Hudibras
D. Autobiography
E. Suspiria De Profoundis
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Romantic essayist Thomas De Quincey authored Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821, A), Autobiographic Sketches (1853, D), and its sequel Suspiria de Profundis (1845, E). The French Revolution is by Thomas Carlyle and Hudibras is by Samuel Butler.

items.title: Q51 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem:
Which of the following works have been written by Thomas Carlyle?
A. Of Heroes and Hero-Worship
B. The French Revolution
C. Of Human Bondage
D. The Hour and the Man
E. Hudibras
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841, A) and The French Revolution: A History (1837, B) were written by Victorian essayist and historian Thomas Carlyle. Of Human Bondage (1915) is by W. Somerset Maugham, The Hour and the Man (1841) is by Harriet Martineau, and Hudibras (1663–78) is by Samuel Butler.

B. Illuminations
C. Syntax and Semantics
D. La revolution du langage poétique
E. The Madwoman in the Attic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Desire in Language: A Semiotic Approach to Literature and Art (1980, A) and La Révolution du langage poétique (Revolution in Poetic Language, 1974, D) were written by Bulgarian-French theorist Julia Kristeva. Illuminations is by Walter Benjamin, and The Madwoman in the Attic is by Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar.

items.title: Q53 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
To which of the following theories New Historicism is indebted?
A. Marxism
B. Formalism
C. Reader-response Theory
D. Existentialism
E. Hermeneutics
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: New Historicism is theoretically indebted to Marxism (A) for its attention to power, ideology, and material history, and to Reader-Response Theory (C) for recognizing that both readers and critics interpret texts from within their own historical and cultural situatedness.

items.title: Q54 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true about cyberpunk?
A. It is a kind of science fiction.
B. It uses postmodernist techniques and posthumanist themes.
C. Events in this novel usually take place within the virtual reality.
D. It is a kind of fiction written using online platforms.
E. The first cyberpunk was written by Thomas Sterne.
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Cyberpunk is a subgenre of science fiction (A) popularized in the 1980s (most famously by William Gibson's Neuromancer, 1984) that employs postmodernist narrative techniques and posthumanist themes (B) and frequently sets its action within virtual reality or cyberspace (C).

items.title: Q55 · March 2023 (Slot 1)

items.explanation: The correctly matched author-novel pairs are Salman Rushdie's The Enchantress of Florence (2008, C), E.L. Doctorow's Ragtime (1975, D), and A.S. Byatt's Possession (1990, E). The Feast of the Goat (2000) was written by Mario Vargas Llosa, and The Autumn of the Patriarch (1975) by Gabriel García Márquez.

items.explanation: R.K. E. Allen Tate – The New Apologists for Poetry
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Crowe Ransom wrote the essay 'Criticism, Inc.' items.title: Q60 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Thomas Rymer
items.stem:
Thomas Rymer coined the term 'poetic justice' to imply the following:
A. the distribution of earthly rewards and punishments in proportion to the virtue or vice of the various characters
B. literary work governed by decorum and morality
C. literary work guided by random ways things often work out in the actual world
D. the metaphysical nature of poetic experience
E. the justification of poetry to be an integral part of the Ideal republic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In The Tragedies of the Last Age Consider'd (1678), Restoration critic Thomas Rymer coined the term 'poetic justice' to argue that drama must distribute earthly rewards to the virtuous and punishments to the wicked in strict proportion (A) and be governed by neoclassical decorum and morality (B).

items.title: Q61 · March 2023 (Slot 1)

items.explanation: Mythologies (1957, B) and The Pleasure of the Text (1973, C) were written by French theorist Roland Barthes. Allegories of Reading (1979) is by Paul de Man, Some Versions of Pastoral (1935) is by William Empson, and 'What Is an Author?' (1969) is by Michel Foucault.

Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Terry Eagleton wrote Criticism and Ideology (1976, C) and Walter Benjamin wrote the essays collected in Illuminations (1968, D). Culture and Society is by Raymond Williams, Literary Theory: A Very Short Introduction is by Jonathan Culler, and The Implied Reader is by Wolfgang Iser.

items.title: Q63 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Which among the following are true in the context of methods and methodologies in literary research?
A. Both are identical in nature.
B. Methods are concerned with how one conducts a given piece of research.
C. Methodologies are concerned with how one conducts a given piece of research.
D. Methodologies are concerned with the perspectives one brings to bear on one's work.
E. Methods are concerned with the perspectives one brings to bear on one's work.
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: As Gabriele Griffin explains in Research Methods for English Studies, research 'methods' are the specific practical techniques or tools used to conduct a given piece of research (B), whereas 'methodologies' refer to the overarching theoretical and philosophical perspectives brought to bear on one's work (D).

items.title: Q64 · March 2023 (Slot 1)

items.explanation: According to the UK English Subject Centre report on postgraduate training in English studies, the essential research skills required are searching skills in libraries (A), editorial skills (B), bibliographic skills (C), and IT skills (E), excluding 'peer management skills' (D).

items.title: Q65 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Which of the following are possible ways of turning a topic into an argument?
A. An argument for or against an existing critic (or critical position) in relation to the author or group of works one is studying.
B. An argument about the value of a new theoretical approach to a text or set of texts.
C. An argument about some historical or literary-historical aspect of literature.
D. An argument showing how a particular theme or concept is not at all related to a group of texts.
E. An argument about the significance of only well-known author/work.
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: In literary research methodology, a general topic is turned into a scholarly argument by arguing for or against an existing critical position (A), demonstrating the value of a new theoretical approach to a text (B), or advancing a claim about a historical or literary-historical aspect of literature (C).

items.title: Q96 · March 2023 (Slot 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Christopher Caudwell
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:
Poetry in its use of language continually distorts and denies the structure of reality to exalt the structure of the self. By means of rhyme, assonance or alliteration it couples together words which have no rational connection, that is, no nexus through the world of external reality. It breaks the word up into lines of arbitrary length, cutting across their logical construction. It breaks down their associations, derived from the world of external reality, by means of inversion and every variety of artificial stressing and counterpoint. Thus the world of external reality recedes and the world of instinct, the affective emotional linkage behind the words, becomes the world of reality... In the novel, too, the subjective elements are valued for themselves, and rise to view, but in a different way. The novel blots out external reality by substituting a more or less consistent mock reality which has sufficient 'stuff' to stand between the reader and reality. This means that in the novel the emotional associations attach not to words but to the moving current of mock reality symbolised by the words. This is why rhythm, 'preciousness', and style are alien to the novel; why the novel translates so well; why novels are not composed of words. They are composed of scenes, actions, stuff, people, just as plays are.

In the above passage, Christopher Caudwell's statement, "Poetry in its use of language continually distorts and denies the structure of reality to exalt the structure of the self" implies:
options: The pragmatic function of poetry that reflects the social reality through expressive language
The capacity of poetry to draw attention to itself as an aesthetic object or artefact
Poetry exalts the "structure of the self" by privileging the notion of the 'egotistical sublime'
The mimetic function of poetry that alludes to the world of external reality in simple, clear language
items.explanation: In this passage from Illusion and Reality (1937), Christopher Caudwell's claim that poetry distorts external reality to 'exalt the structure of the self' implies that poetry privileges subjective, instinctive, ego-centered emotional experience ('the egotistical sublime') over objective external reality.
